Lo
LOH
interjection (KJV vocabulary / prophetic particle)
Old English lā (look! behold! an attention-directing exclamation), cognate with Gothic lai (behold!); survives in Middle English as an emphatic particle of announcement; the Authorized Version uses it to render Hebrew hinneh (הִנֵּה) and Greek idou (ἰδού) where a sudden, solemn disclosure is made — a particle demanding full attention before the utterance that follows.

Biblical Definition

“Lo” is the Authorized Version's most compact particle of divine disclosure — a single syllable that arrests the reader before an utterance of weight. It appears 74 times in the KJV, rendering Hebrew hinneh and Greek idou: two particles signaling “fix your attention here, for what follows is consequential.” The risen Christ's great commission closes with it: “And lo, I am with you always — even to the end of the age” (Matt 28:20). The exclamation is not mere transition; it inaugurates a promise that spans time and eternity, calling every hearer to full awareness before receiving it.

The Song of Songs deploys “lo” in the register of joy: “For lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone” (Song 2:11). The Bride's recognition that a new season has arrived is introduced by a word that says — stop, notice, this matters. In Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, the prophet surveys death before resurrection: “and lo, they were very dry” (Ezek 37:2) — the terrible condition is announced before the LORD's mighty breath transforms it.

The underlying theology of the particle is this: God does not disclose Himself without calling His people to full alertness. The prophetic “lo” is a summons of attention — stop what you are doing, look where God is pointing, and hear what He is saying. The loss of the word in modern translations is the loss of the solemn, arresting tone of prophetic speech.

Webster 1828 Definition

LO: an interjection of attention and disclosure; the Authorized Version's compact particle for “look!” or “behold!”; renders Hebrew hinneh and Greek idou; used in contexts of divine promise (Matt 28:20), prophetic survey (Ezek 37:2), and lyrical recognition (Song 2:11).

expand to see more

LO, interjection. Look! see! behold! An exclamation used to call attention to something presented to view or to the mind.

From Old English lā (an exclamation of attention or surprise); cognate with Gothic lai; survives as the archaic form of “look!” or “behold!” The KJV preserved it as a formal, reverential particle of proclamation.

Webster 1828: “Look! see! behold! A word used to excite attention or to give notice of something about to be seen or observed.”

Distinct from “behold,” which the KJV more often uses in direct-address contexts; “lo” tends toward sudden, compact announcement mid-sentence, as in Matt 28:20 (“and lo”) and Song 2:11 (“for lo”).

Key Scripture

Matt 28:20 — "Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen."

Song 2:11 — "For lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone."

Ezek 37:2 — "And caused me to pass by them round about: and, behold, there were very many in the open valley; and, lo, they were very dry."

Isa 40:9 — "O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain; O Jerusalem, that bringest good tidings, lift up thy voice with strength; lift it up, be not afraid; say unto the cities of Judah, Behold your God!"

Modern Corruption

The elimination of “lo” from modern translations — replaced by nothing, by “look,” or by “behold” inconsistently — strips prophetic speech of its arresting, single-syllable summons and trains readers to receive divine disclosure with casual familiarity rather than alert attention.

expand to see more

Modern translations routinely delete “lo” or replace it with the equally formal “behold” in some places and nothing at all in others. The inconsistency reflects a translational assumption that the particle adds no meaning — that it is merely a stylistic filler the original languages used and English readers can safely ignore. But the prophetic tradition knows otherwise: the attention-particle is not decoration. It is a call to full presence before a disclosure the hearer might otherwise receive half-asleep. The loss of “lo” and “behold” together — a trend in accessibility-driven translations — produces Scripture readings that run headlong into great promises without the arresting pause those promises deserve.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the theology of prophetic attention: God's disclosure demands not passive reception but the alert, halted, fully-present posture of one who has been told “lo — look at this.” Worship that eliminates all formal attention-calling language — in Scripture reading, in prayer, in preaching — creates a devotional culture of casual consumption. The recovery of solemn proclamation particles, whether “lo,” “behold,” or “hearken,” is a liturgical act of reverence toward the God who speaks.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English attention-particle, archaic by 1611; the KJV preserved it as the single-syllable form of “behold” for use in compact, mid-sentence prophetic announcements; renders Hebrew hinneh and Greek idou.

expand to see more

Old English lā — an exclamation of attention or wonder; cognate with Gothic lai; already archaic when the 1611 translators chose it, giving it a solemn, set-apart register

Hebrew hinneh (הִנֵּה) — behold! lo! look!; one of the most frequent particles in the OT, appearing over 1,000 times; signals a disclosure requiring full attention — the LORD's announcement, the prophet's vision, the narrative's turn

Greek idou (ἰδού) — behold! lo! the aorist imperative of horaō (to see); used 200 times in the NT, predominantly in Matthew, Luke-Acts, and Revelation; always marks something worth seeing

The particle-pair “lo — behold” across the Testaments functions liturgically: it trains the reader to pause before the word of the LORD, to treat divine disclosure as announcement rather than information, and to receive it with the posture of a herald's audience rather than a casual reader

Usage

"Charles Spurgeon's preaching regularly paused on prophetic particles. In his sermon on Ezekiel 37 (“The Valley of Dry Bones”), he spent considerable time on the survey — “and lo, they were very dry” — before moving to the resurrection breath. The “lo” forced the hearer to sit in the desolation before receiving the miracle. Spurgeon understood that the solemn attention-particle was not an exegetical accident but a rhetorical and theological necessity: the depth of the problem must be seen before the grace of the solution can be rightly received."

"In the promise of Matt 28:20 — “And lo, I am with you always” — the “lo” carries the weight of the entire commission. The disciples are being sent into the world to make disciples of all nations (v.19), an assignment that would require them to face persecution, rejection, and death. The “lo” before the promise is not decorative; it is a call to attend fully to the only ground on which such a mission is possible: the perpetual covenant presence of the risen Lord."

"The practice of reading Scripture aloud in gathered worship was historically shaped by attention-particles. The reader who says “lo” in a public reading of Matt 28:20 introduces a brief but real pause — a micro-liturgical act — before the promise. The congregation that has learned to hear “lo” as an attention-summons will lean forward slightly at that syllable. The congregation that never hears the word will receive the promise as information rather than as divine disclosure."
